Kurt Wuthrich, PhD: The Wüthrich lab has spent decades pioneering nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to study large biological molecules. Kurt Wüthrich developed methods for determining the 3D structure of proteins and other macromolecules in solution using NMR, work recognized with a Nobel Prize, and later contributed transverse relaxation-optimized spectroscopy (TROSY), which extends NMR to much larger molecular assemblies. Over the years, the group has applied these techniques to questions in cell differentiation, immune suppression, and neuropathology. Today, work continues on two fronts: at ShanghaiTech University, the focus is on how G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) transmit signals across cell membranes; at Scripps Research and ETH Zurich, the group studies healthy aging, particularly how sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss) affects human healthspan. This work matters because NMR remains a key tool for understanding how proteins function at atomic resolution.
Richard Wyatt, PhD: The Wyatt lab works on HIV vaccine design, focusing on the virus's envelope glycoprotein, the target antibodies must recognize to block infection. The lab has engineered stabilized versions of this glycoprotein to make it easier to study its structure and use it in vaccines. In animal studies, vaccine series developed by the lab elicited antibodies in non-human primates capable of neutralizing multiple HIV strains, a step toward a broadly protective vaccine. Related findings show that the ratio of antibodies to viral protein affects how well certain immune cells are engaged, informing how future vaccines should be designed and dosed. This research matters because no effective HIV vaccine yet exists and HIV remains a major global health burden; understanding how to elicit broad, potent antibody responses is central to eventually preventing infection.
John Yates, PhD: The Yates lab develops tools and strategies in proteomics, the large-scale study of proteins, combining mass spectrometry with genomic sequence data. Using peptide tandem mass spectrometry paired with database searching and advanced separation techniques, the lab can directly analyze highly complex mixtures of proteins rather than needing to purify them individually first. This approach has been applied to purified protein complexes as well as to studying how pathogens interact with their hosts, including in diseases like malaria and anthrax. The lab also uses these methods to detect post-translational modifications, chemical changes to proteins after they are made that can alter their function. This work matters because proteins, not just genes, carry out most of a cell's functions, and understanding their identities, interactions, and modifications is essential to understanding both normal biology and disease.
Li Ye, PhD: The Ye lab studies how the brain senses and responds to the body's metabolic state, and how this two-way communication breaks down in disease. Because neurons have high energy demands, the central nervous system is especially sensitive to metabolic stress, and the lab investigates how the brain adapts to both short-term and long-term metabolic changes, and how that adaptation in turn shapes whole-body physiology. To do this, the lab builds and applies advanced imaging tools, including whole-brain tissue clearing (CLARITY/HYBRiD) and large-volume light-sheet microscopy, alongside in vivo calcium imaging and optogenetics to manipulate specific neural circuits, plus high-throughput chemical and genomic screens. The long-term goal is to find brain-based targets for treating metabolic disorders such as obesity and type 2 diabetes, as well as certain neurodegenerative diseases.
Jin-Quan Yu, PhD: The Yu lab is a chemistry group focused on C-H activation, a strategy for building new carbon-carbon and carbon-heteroatom bonds directly from ordinary, unreactive C-H bonds found in simple starting materials like aliphatic acids, amines, and alcohols. By designing catalysts that can selectively break these normally inert bonds, the lab creates shortcuts that drastically shorten the synthesis of drug molecules and other biologically active compounds, aiming to eventually match the precision of enzymes. Research areas include sustainable and asymmetric catalysis, along with applications to natural product and drug synthesis, often in collaboration with computational chemists and pharmaceutical and agrochemical companies. This work matters because more efficient, selective chemical reactions can make drug discovery faster, cheaper, and less wasteful, and trainees learn organometallic chemistry, catalysis, and organic synthesis in a real drug-discovery context.
Meng Zhang, PhD: The Zhang lab studies how cells organize themselves, communicate with each other, and maintain balance within their native tissue environments, and how these processes change with aging and disease. To do this, the lab develops and applies spatial multi-omics tools, methods that map genome-scale information about individual cells while preserving their physical location and context within tissue, combined with advanced imaging and computational analysis. This lets the lab chart how cell states and interactions shift across space and time within a tissue. The long-term goal is to translate these detailed maps of cellular behavior into a better molecular understanding of biology that can support precision medicine, new approaches to treating disease, and cell-based therapies. This matters because many diseases arise not just from single faulty genes but from breakdowns in how cells coordinate within their environment.
Qinghai Zhang, PhD: The Zhang lab studies the chemistry and structural biology of membrane proteins, a class that makes up roughly a third of human genes and more than half of all current drug targets. The lab develops new methods and chemical tools to determine the structure and function of these notoriously difficult-to-study proteins, with particular interest in how they interact with the surrounding lipid membrane and how those interactions affect protein stability and activity. Using structural techniques, the group solves membrane protein structures to understand how drugs bind them and how they work mechanistically, focusing on important classes such as transporters, GPCRs, and ion channels. The lab also develops synthetic chemistry methods to build biologically relevant molecules. This research matters because membrane proteins are central drug targets, and better structural tools can directly speed the discovery of new small-molecule therapeutics.
Jiang Zhu, PhD: The Zhu lab combines computational modeling with experimental validation across several projects in antibody and vaccine research. Using next-generation sequencing and phage display, the lab identifies functional antibodies against viral targets such as HIV-1, RSV, and Zika, and studies how broadly neutralizing antibodies develop naturally or in response to vaccination, using this to design new immunogens and nanoparticle-based vaccines. A separate research line engineers light-sensitive proteins (such as LOV2, PYP, and PHR-CIBN) to optically control neural circuits and signaling pathways relevant to neurodegenerative disease. The lab also builds computational tools to determine the atomic structures of large molecular complexes, like viruses and ion channels, using cryo-electron microscopy data. Together, this work aims to translate structural and computational insight into new strategies for preventing infectious disease and treating neurological disorders.
Eric Zorrilla, PhD: The Zorrilla lab uses rodent models to study the brain mechanisms behind compulsive behaviors, including excessive alcohol and food consumption, and how stress contributes to them. In one study, the lab modeled post-traumatic stress disorder in animals and showed that certain drugs could reduce alcohol preference in that context, pointing to a link between trauma, stress, and drinking behavior. The lab's broader research examines converging vulnerability factors that push both food and drug use toward compulsive patterns, using experimental designs meant to mimic real-life circumstances. By identifying the brain circuits and mechanisms involved, the lab aims to inform more targeted treatments for addiction and stress-related overconsumption. This work matters because substance use disorders and compulsive eating are widespread and often intertwined with trauma, and better mechanistic understanding could lead to more effective therapies.
